mcq.q: Only 2% of tickets are urgent. A model predicting "not urgent" for everything scores…
mcq.why: Accuracy rewards the majority class; recall on the rare class reveals the failure.

mcq.q: How is agreement between two annotators commonly measured?
mcq.why: κ corrects raw agreement for agreement expected by chance. Low agreement means the task is ambiguous, which caps any model.
distractors: Model accuracy is a different question.

mcq.q: Two annotators label 200 tickets and reach κ = 0.58 on “urgent”. What is the right next step?
options: Revise the guideline for the disputed cases before labelling more
Train the model and ignore the disagreement
mcq.why: Disagreement shows the definition is unclear; fix it first or the labels will be noisy.
distractors: More labels from an unclear guideline are more noise.
No model can beat the label ceiling.
The class matters; the guideline needs work.

mcq.q: Which are remedies for class imbalance? Choose all that apply.
mcq.why: Weights, resampling and threshold tuning all help, measured with precision and recall.
distractors: Accuracy hides the rare class: predicting the majority scores high.

mcq.q: You oversample the rare class and then split into train and test. What goes wrong?
options: Copies of the same example land in both train and test, inflating scores
mcq.why: Split first, then resample only the training split.
distractors: Training runs; the evaluation is wrong.

mcq.q: Features must be computed using only information available…
options: At any time, including the future
mcq.why: Anything known only later leaks the answer and fails in production.
distractors: That is exactly the leakage trap.

mcq.q: Why add an is_missing flag instead of only filling missing values?
options: It removes the need for cleaning
mcq.why: Whether a value is missing can correlate with the outcome, so keep that signal.

mcq.q: With 2% positives, what class weight on positives (negatives ÷ positives) balances the classes?
Near-duplicate documents end up split across train and test. What happens to your scores?
options: They look better than they will be in production
mcq.why: The model has effectively seen test examples, which is leakage (3.4).

mcq.q: Why keep raw data immutable?
options: So you can rebuild the training table when code or raw data changes
mcq.why: Each preparation step is versioned code over untouched raw data.
distractors: Labels can be revised; the raw data stays.
It usually costs more space, not less.

interview.q: Why does data quality often matter more than model choice?
covers: Models learn whatever is in the data
Most project time is spent here

interview.q: How do you handle class imbalance?
covers: Use precision, recall and PR curves

interview.q: What makes a good labelling guideline?
Your annotators agree only 60% of the time. What do you do?
covers: Find which cases they disagree on
interview.followUp: When would you accept a low agreement ceiling?

interview.q: Walk through engineering features for a fraud model.
covers: Counts and sums over recent windows
Deviation from the customer's own history
Everything computed as of the prediction time

interview.q: Cancellation labels at {company} are only final after the travel date. How do you build the training set?
covers: Include only bookings whose travel date has passed
Compute features as of booking time
Exclude post-event columns such as fees

interview.q: Design a labelling pipeline for 10,000 support tickets.
covers: Pilot with double labelling and κ

interview.q: Design {company}'s fraud training-data pipeline so it never leaks the label.
covers: No post-event columns such as chargeback flags

mcq.q: Which is leakage when predicting churn on day 3?
mcq.why: Month-total refunds include future information that is not available on day 3.

mcq.q: What is the validation set for?
mcq.why: The test set is held back and used once at the end.

mcq.q: What is overfitting?
options: A model too simple to capture the pattern
Memorising training noise, so training error is low but new-data error is high
mcq.why: Generalisation, performing well on new data, is what matters.

mcq.q: Which of these is not a regularisation technique?
options: Adding more features computed from the label
mcq.why: Features computed from the label are leakage, not regularisation.

mcq.q: A churn model used days since last login, computed at extraction time. Offline AUC was 0.97; in production it was 0.68. What is the fix?
options: Compute features as of the prediction date (a point-in-time join)
mcq.why: For churned customers the feature was large only because they had already left: future information leaked in.
distractors: The threshold does not fix a leaking feature.
A bigger model would exploit the leak even more.

mcq.q: How should you split time-dependent data?
options: Put the newest data in training
Train on the past, test on the future
mcq.why: A random split leaks the future into training.

mcq.q: The same customer appears in both train and test. What split prevents this?
mcq.why: Grouping keeps all of one customer's rows on the same side, so the model cannot memorise their habits.

mcq.q: You check the test set after every change and adjust the model. What happens?
options: The test set quietly becomes validation data, and its estimate is no longer trustworthy
mcq.why: Use the test set once; tune on validation.
distractors: You are fitting to the test set.

mcq.q: What is benchmark contamination for LLMs?
options: Benchmark questions appeared in the pretraining data
mcq.why: If the model saw the questions, its score overstates real ability (8.6).

mcq.q: In the overfitting figure, at a high polynomial degree you raise λ (the ridge penalty). What happens?
options: The curve smooths and validation error recovers
mcq.why: Penalising large weights reduces the wiggles that fit noise.

interview.q: Explain train, validation and test sets, and why each exists.
covers: Test once for a final estimate
Why reusing the test set breaks it

interview.q: What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?
covers: Training error low, new-data error high

interview.q: What is data leakage? Give three examples.
covers: Same user in train and test

interview.q: Offline AUC is 0.97, production 0.68. How do you investigate?
covers: Check each feature's availability at prediction time
Compare offline and online feature values
interview.followUp: Which single check would you do first, and why?

interview.q: How would you split data for a model that predicts customer churn?
covers: Features as of the prediction date

interview.q: {company}'s return model looks perfect offline. What do you check first?
covers: Columns filled after delivery, such as refund amounts
A random split mixing sale and non-sale periods

interview.q: Design an evaluation protocol that prevents leakage for a time-dependent problem.
How do you prevent test-set overuse in a team that iterates quickly?
covers: Restrict access to the final test set
Use validation and cross-validation for iteration

mcq.q: When is a PR curve more informative than ROC?
mcq.why: With rare positives, ROC can look good while precision is poor; PR curves expose that.

mcq.q: A classifier has 40 true positives, 10 false positives and 20 false negatives. What is its precision?
mcq.why: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 40/50 = 80%.

mcq.q: With the same counts (TP 40, FP 10, FN 20), what is recall?
mcq.why: Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 40/60 ≈ 67%.
distractors: That is not a standard ratio here.

mcq.q: A model has precision 0.9 and recall 0.3. What is its F1?
mcq.why: F1 = 2PR/(P + R) = 2(0.9)(0.3)/1.2 = 0.45. The harmonic mean is pulled towards the weaker of the two, so F1 is high only if both are high.
distractors: That is the plain average; F1 is the harmonic mean.
That is the product P × R.

mcq.q: A ROC AUC of 0.5 means…
options: The model ranks no better than random
mcq.why: AUC 0.5 is random ranking; 1.0 is perfect.

mcq.q: What does it mean for a model to be calibrated?
options: Among cases scored 0.8, about 80% are positive
mcq.why: Calibration is checked with a reliability diagram and summarised by expected calibration error.
distractors: The threshold is a separate choice.

mcq.q: A missed fraud costs $400 and a false alarm costs $5 of analyst time. Where will the cost-minimising threshold sit?
options: It cannot be chosen from costs
mcq.why: Misses are 80 times more expensive than false alarms, so catching more fraud is worth more alerts.
distractors: That would minimise false alarms, the cheap error.
Sweeping thresholds against expected cost is exactly how to choose it.

mcq.q: If a false alarm instead blocks a customer's card, costing about $60 in churn, what happens to the best threshold?
mcq.why: False alarms are now more expensive, so the optimum trades some recall for precision.
distractors: Higher false-alarm cost pushes it up, not down.

mcq.q: Platt scaling or isotonic regression for calibration should be fitted on…
mcq.why: Fitting on training data reuses the same overconfident predictions; the test set must stay untouched.
distractors: The test set is for the final estimate.

mcq.q: An escalation classifier must keep precision at or above 80% because reviewers have limited time. How should the threshold be chosen?
mcq.why: The product requirement is a precision floor; F1 can pick a threshold that breaks it.

interview.q: Explain precision, recall and F1, and when each matters.
covers: Precision: how many flagged are right
Recall: how many true cases are caught
Choose by the cost of each error

interview.q: When is a PR curve more useful than a ROC curve?
covers: ROC can look good while precision is poor
PR shows the alerts a team will actually see

interview.q: What does calibration mean, and how do you check it?
covers: Platt or isotonic on validation data

interview.q: Choose a threshold for a fraud model given the cost of a miss and of a false alarm.
interview.followUp: What changes if analysts can only review 500 alerts a day?

interview.q: Your model's AUC is 0.95, but users complain about false alarms. Explain.
covers: At a low base rate, precision can still be poor
Look at precision at the chosen threshold
Adjust the threshold or improve the model on the rare class

interview.q: {company} holds refunds for manual review when abuse risk is high. How do you set the threshold?
covers: Cost of delaying an honest refund versus a lost item
Monitor precision and complaints after launch

interview.q: Design a metrics dashboard for a classifier in production.
covers: Precision and recall at the operating threshold

interview.q: How would you decide whether an LLM's self-reported confidence can trigger automatic actions?
covers: A labelled set of right and wrong outputs
Reliability diagram for the stated confidence

mcq.q: Supervised learning learns from…
mcq.why: Examples: email → spam or not spam, house features → price.

mcq.q: Self-supervised learning gets its labels from…
options: The data itself, for example by hiding the next word and predicting it
mcq.why: Because the labels come free from the text, pretraining can use trillions of tokens.
distractors: Rules do not produce training labels here.

mcq.q: Why can LLM pretraining use trillions of tokens without human labelling?
options: It is self-supervised: the next token is the label
mcq.why: Every position in the text provides its own target, so no annotation is needed.
distractors: Human labelling at that scale would be impossible.
RL is used later, in post-training (6.5).
It needs enormous amounts of text.

mcq.q: In reinforcement learning, what does the agent learn?
options: A policy that maximises total reward from its actions in an environment
mcq.why: The agent acts, receives rewards and adjusts its policy to collect more reward.

mcq.q: You want to discover customer segments with no labels at all. Which paradigm fits?
mcq.why: With no answers to learn from, you look for structure in the inputs.
distractors: There are no labels to supervise with.
There is no reward for actions here.
You do not know the segments well enough to write rules.

mcq.q: A shop chooses which homepage layout to show and is rewarded by clicks. Which paradigm is this?
options: A bandit, a simple form of reinforcement learning
mcq.why: The system takes an action (a layout), observes a reward (clicks) and shifts towards better actions.
distractors: There is no fixed label per example; feedback comes from actions taken.
Pretraining predicts hidden parts of data.
There is a reward, so it is not unsupervised.

mcq.q: Predicting whether an order will be returned, from past orders with known outcomes, is…
mcq.why: Past orders with returned or not-returned outcomes are labelled examples.
distractors: It is a standard ML problem.
Nothing is acting to collect rewards.

mcq.q: A multi-step LLM agent tries tools until a task is done. Is that reinforcement learning?
options: Only if it runs on GPUs
No, unless its weights are actually updated from a reward signal
mcq.why: Trying options at inference time is a control loop. RL means learning from reward by changing weights.

mcq.q: What is the main difference between the learning paradigms?
options: The feedback signal: correct answers, no answers, or a score for actions
mcq.why: The paradigm is defined by what the learner is told, not by the model type.
distractors: Any paradigm can be written in any language.
Models of any size can use any paradigm.
Hardware does not define the paradigm.

mcq.q: Detecting unusual transactions with no fraud labels yet is an example of…
mcq.why: Without labels, you flag inputs that differ from the bulk of the data.
distractors: This is not predicting hidden parts of text.

interview.q: Explain supervised, unsupervised, self-supervised and reinforcement learning, with one example each.
Why is LLM pretraining called self-supervised?
covers: The next token is the label
Later stages add supervised and RL tuning

interview.q: What is the feedback signal in each paradigm, and why does it matter for data collection?
covers: The signal decides what you can learn

interview.q: You have no labels for a new support category. What can you do?
covers: Weak labels from rules or an LLM

interview.q: When is a bandit the right tool, and what are its risks?
covers: Choosing among options with fast feedback
Guardrails for fairness and loss limits

interview.q: Fraud labels at {company} arrive weeks after the payment. How would you combine supervised and unsupervised methods?
covers: Unsupervised anomaly signals for new patterns

interview.q: Design a system that discovers new complaint themes each week and routes them.
covers: Human review names and merges clusters
Promote stable themes to supervised classes
Close the loop with routing rules

interview.q: A team proposes RL to tune an assistant against live customer conversations. What would you require first?
covers: A reward that cannot be gamed easily
Offline evaluation before any live exposure
Clear limits on what it may change

mcq.q: Regression predicts…
options: A number, such as a price or delivery time
mcq.why: Linear regression fits y = w·x + b by minimising squared error.

mcq.q: How does logistic regression produce a decision?
options: It outputs a probability through the sigmoid, and a threshold turns it into a decision
mcq.why: σ(z) = 1/(1 + e^−z) gives a probability; the threshold is a separate choice (3.5).
distractors: Trees are a different model family.
The output is a probability; the decision needs a threshold.

mcq.q: What is σ(0), the sigmoid of zero?
distractors: σ approaches 1 only for very positive inputs.
σ approaches 0 only for very negative inputs.
The sigmoid's output is between 0 and 1.

mcq.q: What two steps does k-means alternate?
options: Assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points
mcq.why: It stops when assignments stop changing.
distractors: That is not how clustering works.

mcq.q: How does gradient boosting differ from a random forest?
options: Boosting adds trees one at a time, each correcting the previous errors; a forest averages independent trees
mcq.why: Forests average many trees on random subsets; boosting stacks trees on residual errors.
distractors: A single deep tree overfits; boosting uses many shallow ones.

mcq.q: For tabular data, which is usually the strongest practical choice?
mcq.why: Gradient boosting usually wins on structured tables.
distractors: LLMs are costly and poorly calibrated for tabular scoring.

mcq.q: 88% of tickets are “general”. A classifier reports 91% accuracy. What is the real gain over the majority-class baseline?
mcq.why: Always predicting “general” already scores 88%, so the model adds 3 points, and rare-class recall may still be poor.
distractors: That compares with 82%, which is not the baseline.

mcq.q: A sophisticated model barely beats a simple baseline. What should you conclude?
options: It is not adding much value yet; look at per-class results and costs
Accuracy is the only thing that matters
mcq.why: Report the baseline next to every result; if the gain is tiny, the complexity may not be worth it.
distractors: A tiny gain may not justify the cost.
Per-class metrics matter, especially for rare classes.
The baseline is a reference, not an error.

mcq.q: In the k-means figure, you choose a k that does not match the true groups. What happens?
options: It finds the true number of groups automatically
mcq.why: k-means always produces k clusters, so clean-looking clusters do not prove real structure.
distractors: Points are spread across all k centres.
k must be chosen; it is not discovered.

mcq.q: A tuned model is measured on validation data, and the baseline on a different test set. What is wrong?
options: The comparison is unfair: both must be measured on the same data
The baseline should not be measured
mcq.why: Different data gives different difficulty; compare like with like.
distractors: It can make either look better than it is.
The baseline is what keeps you honest.
Difficulty depends on the data, not the split's name.

interview.q: Compare regression, classification and clustering, with an example of each.
How does k-means work, and what are its limitations?
covers: Assumes roughly round clusters and is sensitive to scale

interview.q: Explain the difference between random forests and gradient boosting.
covers: Averaging independent trees versus sequential residual fitting
Boosting usually stronger on tabular data

interview.q: Why should you always report a baseline? Which baselines would you use for a ticket router?
covers: Shows whether the model adds value

interview.q: Your classifier is 91% accurate. What else do you need to know before you trust it?
Build a first return-prediction model for {company}. Which baseline and model do you start with, and how do you judge them?
covers: Majority-class and a simple rule baseline
Recall at a usable precision, not accuracy

interview.q: Design a model-selection process for a tabular problem with a strict deadline.
covers: One primary metric agreed up front

interview.q: When would you use an LLM instead of a gradient-boosted model for classification, and how would you compare them fairly?
covers: Unstructured text and few labels favour LLMs
Consider using the LLM to create labels for a cheaper model

mcq.q: What does error analysis involve?
options: Sampling failures, tagging each with a cause, counting buckets and fixing the largest
Re-running training with a new seed
mcq.why: The biggest bucket, weighted by impact, tells you what to fix next.
distractors: Size rarely fixes the biggest bucket.
A new seed does not explain failures.

mcq.q: Why compute metrics per slice?
options: An overall average can hide a group where the model fails badly
mcq.why: A model at 89% overall may be far worse on mixed-language or new-product inputs.
distractors: Slices are views of the test set.

mcq.q: Hyperparameters should be tuned on…
mcq.why: Touch the test set once; tune on validation.
distractors: Production needs labels and carries risk.
Tuning on test data overfits to it.

mcq.q: Why is random search often better than grid search per trial?
options: It always finds the global optimum
It explores more distinct values of the hyperparameters that matter
mcq.why: When only a few hyperparameters matter, random sampling tries more of their values in the same budget.
distractors: Random search is random by design.

mcq.q: Covariate shift means…
options: The inputs change, for example a new customer region
The relationship between inputs and labels changes
mcq.why: The input distribution moves, so the model sees regions it rarely trained on.
distractors: That is label or prior shift.

mcq.q: Fraud suddenly spikes from 0.5% to 2% of transactions with the same tactics. This is…
mcq.why: The class balance changed; the input-label relationship did not.
distractors: Concept drift would mean new tactics.
The question is about class balance.

mcq.q: Fraudsters adopt a new tactic that old features do not capture. This is…
mcq.why: The relationship between inputs and the label has changed.
distractors: Overfitting is about training, not the world changing.
Inputs may look normal while the meaning changes.

mcq.q: A document classifier drops from 92% to 84% after scanned PDFs rise from 5% to 30% of traffic. What does the topic recommend?
options: Improve OCR, add scanned samples to training and add a scanned slice to the dashboard
Switch to a larger model only
mcq.why: Error analysis showed most new errors were scanned documents, so fix data and monitor that slice.
distractors: An 8-point drop with a known cause needs action.
The fix is data, not size.

mcq.q: An input-drift alarm fires. What is the right first response?
options: Measure performance; drift is a reason to check, not proof that accuracy fell
mcq.why: Inputs can drift without harming accuracy, and accuracy can fall without visible input drift.
distractors: Retraining blindly can make things worse.

mcq.q: When is cross-validation most useful?
mcq.why: It reuses scarce data for more reliable estimates; with lots of data a single validation split is often enough.
distractors: It applies to many model types.
With lots of data it is often unnecessary.
It is a standard tuning tool.

interview.q: Describe the error-analysis loop.
covers: Fix the biggest, often in the data
Re-evaluate on the same test set and slices

interview.q: Explain the difference between covariate shift, label shift and concept drift.
covers: Detection and response differ for each

interview.q: How should you tune hyperparameters without fooling yourself?
Accuracy dropped eight points last month. Walk through your investigation.
covers: Confirm the drop and its timing
Slice by segment and input type
Check input drift and data pipeline changes
interview.followUp: How would you tell a data-pipeline bug from real-world drift?

interview.q: Why is random search often better than grid search?
covers: Random covers more values of those
Bayesian optimisation as a next step

interview.q: Recall on UPI payments at {company} fell in November while the inputs looked normal. What happened, and what do you do?
covers: Likely concept drift from a new tactic
Find it by slicing labelled outcomes

interview.q: Design drift monitoring for a model whose labels arrive weeks late.
covers: Input statistics as an early signal
Clear runbook for when to retrain

interview.q: Monsoon disruptions break {company}'s cancellation model every year. Design a process so they do not.
covers: Slice dashboards by route and month
